claims.text: A stable Cr-rich passivating oxide film is chiefly responsible for enhanced corrosion resistance in Fe–Cr–Ni steels under corrosive and irradiative conditions.
A radiation-tolerant microstructure is a principal contributor to the corrosion resistance of irradiated Fe–Cr–Ni steels.
The controlled study uses homogenized Fe–Cr–Ni steels containing at least 10 wt% Cr and having documented grain size and phase distributions.
The proposed exposure combines a high-temperature corrosive medium with a controlled radiation flux and monitors oxide and microstructural evolution using nanotomography and electron microscopy.
Pressurized water or other corrosive media at temperatures up to approximately 600 °C and service-relevant radiation levels represent chemical-processing or nuclear-reactor environments.
The relevant structural mediator is a dense, adherent Cr-rich passive oxide film.
A fine-grained Fe–Cr–Ni matrix is radiation tolerant.
Chromium preferentially oxidizes and becomes the principal former of the passive oxide film.
The Cr-rich oxide is compact and protective, resisting dissolution and retarding corrosion.
Stable grain boundaries and second-phase nanoparticles act as sinks for irradiation-induced defects.
Defect-sink microstructural features limit radiation damage and thereby maintain oxide-film integrity.
Steels retaining stable Cr-rich oxide layers with minimal irradiation-induced disruption will corrode more slowly and sustain less damage than low-Cr or less radiation-tolerant steels.
Low-Cr steels are expected to form less protective oxide films and show higher corrosion rates or oxide breakdown.
Steels tested under milder thermal and non-irradiative conditions are expected to form less protective oxides and exhibit greater corrosion or film breakdown.
The hypothesized mechanism applies primarily to Fe–Cr–Ni steels containing approximately 10–20 wt% Cr at temperatures no higher than 600 °C and at moderate radiation doses.
At extreme temperatures or radiation doses, mechanisms other than Cr-rich passivation and defect-sink stabilization may dominate.
The long-term stability of passivating oxide layers under prolonged or very high irradiation is insufficiently characterized.
Failure of Cr-bearing steels to show improved oxide stability or lower corrosion rates than lower-Cr controls under identical irradiation would falsify the proposed role of the Cr-rich passive film.

contradictions.description: The baseline predicts poorer passivation and greater corrosion under milder, non-irradiative conditions, whereas the mechanism and uncertainty fields treat irradiation and severe exposure as sources of damage that threaten oxide integrity. Without another changed variable, the expected direction for the milder control is inconsistent.
